name: Central Carrier
confidence_why: Story 1989, the only first-hand description of Central Carrier stress, puts a breath-force stress on the stem syllable independently of the word's single high pitch accent, Gessner 2002 accepts that account and measures longer verb-stem syllables in the Lheidli dialect, and McDonough 1990, working from Pike's 1986 data, treats the language as pitch accent without discussing stress at all, so the record rests on few sources but nothing read contradicts it. Dakelh is described separately below; the pattern is the same.

catalog_quote: [Story 1989:100] Central Carrier is on the border between a language characterized by accent and one characterized by tone. 'Accent' or 'stress' is the better term when single words are considered in their surface forms since a word carries one and only one 'accent'. However, when words (or morphemes) are juxtaposed, then ... perturbations occur which are much more characteristic of a tone language. ... First, there is a phonemic stress which is defined in terms of breath force and which is independent of high tone (pitch accent). It is phonemic since within the phonological word, the location of the syllable carrying stress is unpredictable. Phonological words are not in one-to-one correspondence with grammatical words. sweep_summary: Two title-hits for Central Carrier, both obtained and read, neither about Carrier word stress. Leer 1976 (ANLA CA965L1976b, 86-page scan downloaded from ANLA and scanned page by page) is a comparative Athabaskan tonogenesis manuscript; Carrier occurs only as a column in stem-reflex charts and 'stress'/'accent' never occur — silent on the catalog's classification. Hargus 2003 (ANLA CA982H2003, typescript of Hargus 2005 in Athabaskan Prosody; already held under babi1235, copied into carr1249) is on Witsuwit'en and Fort Ware Sekani stress; Central Carrier is named once (typescript p. 26 + fn. 18) as a possible test case for tone-stress interaction, with no placement statement — silent. No first-hand Central Carrier stress statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title, so the catalog's deciding source (Story 1989:100, stem-final stress with a culminative pitch accent; classification 'morphological') stands unchanged; our earlier reading's open list of works to obtain (Gessner 2002 ANLC WP2 soft-404; Walker 1979 and Pike 1986 paywalled; Morice 1932 controlled lending) is untouched.

new_statements.quote: [p.ii] One of the findings is that in addition to word-final stress in verbs, manifested primarily in terms of duration, "prominence" in the form of increased pitch is typically also found on one of the earlier syllables in the word. The location of the latter is partly determined phonologically, and in part lexically; certain prefixes appear to carry lexical tone [...] [p.182] Dakelh does indeed seem to have both stress and tone, which appear to operate independently of each other. Stress is manifested as increased duration, and can be observed on verb stem syllables. As was argued in chapter 2, this is the head syllable of an obligatory uneven iamb (a bisyllabic light-heavy sequence), aligned with the right edge of the stem.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (cued by vowel duration) falls on the verb-stem syllable, which is the final syllable of the verb (and of deverbal nouns); it is the strong member of a light-heavy iamb aligned with the right edge of the stem. Independently of this, every word carries one high tone (culminative H, partly lexical, on certain prefixes), realised as a pitch peak on an earlier syllable in verbs and on either syllable of bisyllabic nouns. Alternative coding: tone language with a stress statement (Gessner treats Dakelh as a combined stress + tone system).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress stated. Instead a separate pitch prominence (H tone): in polysyllabic (deverbal) nouns usually one prefix syllable is prominent by raised pitch (and some duration), preferentially on incorporated lexical items, lexically toned morphemes, closed syllables and full vowels (pp.141-142).
new_statements.exceptions: Mono- and bisyllabic nouns show only pitch prominence, not durational stress; in bisyllabic nouns the location of H is contrastive (HL, LH, HH; p.142, p.182). Bird 2002 (per Gessner p.105) found most Lheidli bisyllables (79/111) with initial 'stress' cued by pitch and amplitude, not duration. Generalisations for prefix prominence are called preliminary (p.142).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolation/citation forms elicited from three Lheidli speakers; verbs and deverbal nouns vs. underived nouns treated separately; sentence-level prosody and tone sandhi handled in separate sections (3.3, ch.4).
new_statements.identity_note: Statement describes the Lheidli dialect (Lheidli T'enneh, Prince George), which Poser 1999b / YDLI / Gessner 2003:3 place in the Fraser-Nechakoh group of the Southern subgroup of Dakelh (= ISO caf Southern Carrier, Glottolog sout2958). Glottolog 5.3 lists only Blackwater Carrier (blac1272) as a named dialect child of sout2958, so the Lheidli assignment rests on the ISO/Poser classification, not on a Glottolog dialect node. Central Carrier carr1249 (Nak'azdli/Stuart Lake; Story 1989, Pike 1986, Walker 1979, Morice 1932) is a separate catalog entry already; no first-hand stress description of the Blackwater/Ulkatcho dialects was found (Poser's Ulkatcho and Saik'uz materials are silent on stress and tone).

new_statements.quote: First of all, Dakelh does indeed seem to have both stress and tone, which appear to operate independently of each other. Stress is manifested as increased duration, and can be observed on verb stem syllables. As was argued in chapter 2, this is the head syllable of an obligatory uneven iamb (a bisyllabic light-heavy sequence), aligned with the right edge of the stem. Tone, which is entirely independent of this stress, is manifested by raised pitch. ... Every word appears to have at least one high-toned syllable ... In bisyllabic nouns the location of high tone appears to be contrastive. Verbs, and deverbal nouns, generally have tone on their first or second syllable.
new_statements.citation: Gessner, Suzanne C. 2003. The prosodic system of the Dakelh (Carrier) language. PhD dissertation, University of British Columbia.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.15 Chapter summary, p.182 (Lheidli dialect; supported by sec. 2.14 p.51, sec. 3.8.2 p.147, sec. 3.10 p.156, sec. 5.1 p.254)
new_statements.reading: Lheidli (Southern Carrier): verbs have fixed stress on the stem syllable, which is always the final syllable of the verb (p.156), cued by vowel duration (stem 140 ms vs prefix 102 ms, p<.0001, p.147) and analysed as a right-aligned uneven iamb; a separate culminative H tone (pitch), lexically specified on some morphemes and otherwise phonologically placed, sits usually on the first or second syllable of verbs and is contrastive in bisyllabic nouns; nouns of one or two syllables show only pitch prominence, no durational stress. So: fixed final (stem) stress in verbs plus an independent lexical/pitch accent H tone — a mixed stress-tone system, not a free-stress one. Earlier sources relayed by Gessner agree on final/stem stress (Morice 1932:7, Story 1984:24, Prunet 1990, Story 1989:100), while Bird 2002:92 found predominantly initial pitch/amplitude prominence in Lheidli bisyllables (79/111).

new_statements.quote: p.121: "While other languages of the Athabascan family exhibit either tone or stress, Dakelh has been reported to have a combination of pitch accent and stress (Pike 1986, Story 1989, Poser 1992)." [...] "She reports that Dakelh exhibits both stress and a type of tone. Each word in isolation carries a single "accent" or high (H) tone. There is a sharp drop in pitch between a syllable carrying H tone and the immediately following syllable. Each syllable preceding the H-toned syllable is also realized with H tone." p.123: "Underlyingly toneless nouns are assigned a high tone due to the requirement that each phonological word have a tone on the surface. This default H is always inserted at the right edge of the root."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Central Carrier has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so nothing to contradict. Gessner 2002 supplies a typed statement: a pitch accent (one H per word) system with stress-like correlates, accent position lexical (underlying H on initial or final syllable, default H at the right edge of the root for toneless words), plus tone-sandhi lowering. The Nak'albun data are Central Carrier proper (Stuart Lake, Fort St. James); the Lheidli data are a Prince George variety that Poser 2017 (held by the project in this folder, pp. 44-45) groups with the Fraser-Nechako division of Southern Carrier, so the Lheidli findings are only partly about carr1249.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dakelh is described (following Story 1989, Pike 1986, Poser 1992) as a mixed pitch accent-plus-stress system, not a plain stress or tone language. In the Nak'albun (Stuart Lake) dialect every word in isolation carries exactly one 'accent' (H tone); all syllables before it are also H and there is a sharp pitch drop right after it. The accent's position is lexical: nouns descending from Proto-Athabaskan constricted-vowel forms have an underlying H on the initial or the final syllable (CV'CV or CVCV'), while underlyingly toneless words receive a default H at the right edge of the root (i.e. on the stem's last syllable). Tone sandhi lowers the H of a following transitive verb, noun (after a numeral) or enclitic after an underlyingly H noun, but not after a toneless noun. In the Lheidli (Prince George) dialect (p.124) only one syllable per word is prominent, but pre-accent syllables are not all H (LH and LHL attested), monosyllables are always H, pitch is relative rather than categorical (p.126: 'This type of variation may be more indicative of a stress language'), and verb-stem syllables are significantly longer ('This may also be a correlate of stress'); the summary (p.133) says Lheidli 'exhibits several stress-like properties (relative pitch, differences in duration)'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the paper describes a single prominent (H-accented) syllable per word and says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect and speaker variation: Lheidli shows an LH pattern absent from Nak'albun (e.g. duné 'man', duchún 'tree'), some Nak'albun HH words are HL in Lheidli (ts'éke 'woman', kétul 'sock'), and Lheidli speaker B shows no lowering in [object noun]+[transitive verb] contexts, only in [noun]+[clitic]. Story (1989) notes no tone perturbation in [subject noun]+[object noun] or [subject noun]+[intransitive verb] (p.122 fn.3). Onset type affects pitch (lenis onsets lower, p.125); sentence-final words are extra-low and isolation forms fall on the final syllable (p.124), which can obscure underlying tone on sentence-final verbs (p.127).
new_statements.identity_note: Gessner 2002 compares two Dakelh dialects. The Nak'albun data (from Story 1989, speaker Francesca Antoine, Fort St. James) are the Stuart Lake dialect, the core of Central Carrier [carr1249]. The new fieldwork data are the Lheidli dialect (Prince George, fewer than ten speakers in 2002, speakers Margaret Gagnon and Mary Gouchie); Poser 2017 (The Carrier Language: A Brief Introduction, pp. 44-45, file in the same check folder) places Lheidli T'enneh in the Fraser-Nechako group of Southern Carrier, not Stuart Lake. The pitch accent statement quoted from p.121 is about Dakelh generally and the Nak'albun dialect specifically; the stress-like observations (pp. 124-126, 133) are about Lheidli.

tone_statements.quote: although words elicited in isolation do not suggest a lexical tone contrast, the same is not true once those words are put in a syntactic context. ... In Nak'azdli, a lexical tone may be located on any one of a word's syllables; this means that not only presence vs. absence of lexical tone, but also the location of that lexical tone, is fully contrastive. ... In both dialects, a default high tone is inserted on underlyingly toneless words ... In the Nak'azdli dialect, default high is inserted on the rightmost syllable of the word, and spreads to each preceding syllable.

tone_statements.summary: Privative H pitch accent-like system: lexical /H/ vs. toneless, one surface H per word (default H on final syllable of the morphological word in Nak'azdli), leftward H spread, post-H fall; contrast diagnosed by tone sandhi (H-lowering of following word); plus independent word-final (stem) stress.

tone_statements.citation: Story, Gillian L (1985-05-20). Letter to Michael Krauss Concerning Carrier Tone.
tone_statements.quote: The tone rules are working out very nicely within the verb prefix string. … the distributive prefix ya does not carry a basic high tone in Carrier … There is no difficulty with prefix strings which contain no basic high tone; then the tone occurs on the stem syllable. But if a basic high tone occurs immediately before the stem syllable, then the ultimate tone placement seems to depend on the paradigm. … There is evidence for semelfactive-transitional ɬ́, the basic high tone attested by the fact that it blocks the rightward shift of a basic high tone on a syllable immediately to the left.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1, paragraphs 3-4 and p. 3, paragraph beginning 'There is evidence'
tone_statements.summary: Verb prefixes either carry a basic high tone or none; a basic high shifts one syllable rightward, and with no high in the prefix string the tone falls on the stem syllable. Only high named; no count.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources: only one work was listed and opened. Within Gessner 2002 the two dialects differ: Nak'albun (Story 1989) has HH/HL surface patterns with every pre-accent syllable H and regular sandhi lowering, while Lheidli adds an LH pattern, does not raise all pre-accent syllables, shows relative rather than categorical pitch and longer verb-stem syllables (stress-like), and one of two Lheidli speakers shows no noun-verb lowering at all. The paper's own framing ('a combination of pitch accent and stress'; Story: 'both stress and a type of tone') means the label tone language with a stress statement would also be defensible; pitch accent is chosen because the paper's core generalization is one H 'accent' per word with predictable spreading to preceding syllables.

sources.quote: Reanalysis of Pike (1986) Nak'azdli data: 'Carrier is a pitch accent language with a system like Japanese. The syllable is the bearer of accent and every word has a high tone, either by assigning the high tone to the accented syllable or by a default rule which assigns a high tone to the final syllable of a word ... The contrast in Carrier is between accented vs unaccented morphemes.' No statement about breath-force stress or its location (the word 'stress' occurs only in a Beckman 1986 title).

sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei. ... In the case of Athabaskan, however, the development of tone depended not only on the vowel nucleus, but on the final consonant of the syllable. If the final consonant was glottalized, the reflex of the tone is opposite of what it is if the final consonant was not glottalized.

sources.note: Comparative-historical paper on Athabaskan tonogenesis (stem vowel nuclei, glottalized stem-final consonants, spirantization). Carrier appears only as a column in the correspondence charts (Chart 4 syllable-type reflexes; Chart 5 stem-final consonant reflexes) and in a marginal note citing Morice. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the 86-page scanned; nothing on where word stress or the pitch accent falls in Carrier.

tone.quote: Nevertheless, it did seem that Central Carrier tonality is much more than sentence- or word-stress; it gives the impression that Carrier is at least to some extent a tone language. … He notes “it would be misleading to call Carrier a tone language” … where it seems rather that certain syllables or morphemes sometimes, usually, or almost always (never quite always?) exhibit high-pitched accent. … Cook at least makes a first attempt to discuss the problem, which is still very far from being solved.

tone.quote: The tone rules are working out very nicely within the verb prefix string. … the distributive prefix ya does not carry a basic high tone in Carrier … There is no difficulty with prefix strings which contain no basic high tone; then the tone occurs on the stem syllable. But if a basic high tone occurs immediately before the stem syllable, then the ultimate tone placement seems to depend on the paradigm. … There is evidence for semelfactive-transitional ɬ́, the basic high tone attested by the fact that it blocks the rightward shift of a basic high tone on a syllable immediately to the left.
tone.locator: p. 1, paragraphs 3-4 and p. 3, paragraph beginning 'There is evidence'
tone.summary: Verb prefixes either carry a basic high tone or none; a basic high shifts one syllable rightward, and with no high in the prefix string the tone falls on the stem syllable. Only high named; no count.
tone.says: Verb prefixes either carry a basic high tone or none; a basic high shifts one syllable rightward, and with no high in the prefix string the tone falls on the stem syllable. Only high named; no count.
